group.title: Media and journalism
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: An article that gives the official opinion of a newspaper’s editors.
examples: Today’s {editorial} criticizes the new housing policy.
wrong: The editorial was a neutral list of facts with no opinion at all.

words.meaning: A journalist who reports from a particular place or on a particular subject.
examples: Our {correspondent} in Tokyo sent this report.
wrong: The correspondent never reports on anything; she only reads the weather.

words.meaning: The way news media report on an event, and how much they report.
examples: The election received wall-to-wall {coverage} on every channel.
wrong: The story got huge coverage, so almost nobody heard about it.

words.meaning: The quality of reporting facts fairly, without letting personal feelings shape them.
examples: Readers trust the paper because of its {objectivity}.
wrong: His objectivity showed in how he let his own opinions shape every story.

words.meaning: Presenting news in a shocking, exaggerated way to attract attention.
examples: The tabloid was criticized for its {sensationalism} about the crash.
wrong: The calm, careful report was a fine example of sensationalism.

words.meaning: A small-format newspaper with short stories, big photos and much celebrity gossip.
examples: The {tabloids} were full of rumors about the singer’s wedding.
wrong: The tabloid is known for long, serious analysis of economic policy.

words.meaning: A large-format newspaper known for serious news and in-depth reporting.
examples: The {broadsheet} ran a ten-page analysis of the budget.
wrong: The broadsheet is famous for celebrity gossip and shocking headlines.

words.meaning: An important news story that one reporter or paper publishes before anyone else.
examples: The young reporter got the {scoop} on the minister’s resignation.
wrong: Her scoop was old news that every paper had printed a week earlier.

words.meaning: Saying clearly where a fact, quote or idea came from.
examples: Every quote in the article needs a clear {attribution} to its source.
wrong: The attribution hid the name of the person who wrote the quote.

words.meaning: The office where journalists and editors prepare the news.
examples: The {newsroom} went quiet as the election results came in.
wrong: The newsroom is the place where readers sit to read the paper.

words.meaning: To check that the facts in a piece of writing or a speech are correct.
examples: Every claim in the article was {fact-checked} before publication.
wrong: She fact-checked the story by publishing it without reading it.

words.meaning: A public statement that something published earlier was wrong and is withdrawn.
examples: The paper printed a {retraction} after the story proved false.
wrong: The retraction repeated the false claim and said it was completely true.

words.meaning: A false written statement that damages someone’s reputation, which can be punished by law.
examples: The actor sued the magazine for {libel}.
wrong: Printing a true, fair report is a clear example of libel.

words.meaning: The control or blocking of books, news or films that authorities think are unacceptable.
examples: Under strict {censorship}, many news stories never reached the public.
wrong: Thanks to censorship, every newspaper could print anything it wanted.

words.meaning: The right of newspapers and broadcasters to report without control by the government.
examples: Journalists marched to defend {press freedom}.
wrong: Press freedom means the government decides what newspapers may print.

words.meaning: Biased or false information spread to make people support a particular cause or leader.
examples: The posters were wartime {propaganda} meant to stir up hatred.
wrong: The propaganda gave a balanced view of both sides.

words.meaning: A way of presenting information that makes it look better for a particular person or group.
examples: The minister’s press team put a positive {spin} on the bad figures.
wrong: There was no spin in the statement; it twisted every fact in their favor.

words.meaning: False or wrong information, especially when it is spread without people realizing it.
examples: Health {misinformation} spread quickly during the outbreak.
wrong: The misinformation was accurate and carefully checked.

words.meaning: An opinion article in a newspaper written by someone who is not on the paper’s staff.
examples: The professor wrote an {op-ed} arguing for longer school days.
wrong: An op-ed is a page that only lists sports results.

words.meaning: A journalist who writes regular articles giving their opinions.
examples: The {columnist} writes about politics every Sunday.
wrong: As a columnist, she has never shared her opinion in print.

words.meaning: Involving careful, long research to discover hidden facts, often about wrongdoing.
examples: Her {investigative} reporting exposed corruption in the city council.
wrong: His investigative work never looked beyond the official press release.

words.meaning: A line at the top of an article that gives the writer’s name.
examples: It was her first front-page story with her own {byline}.
wrong: The byline is the price of the newspaper printed on the front.

words.meaning: The number of copies of a newspaper or magazine sold or given out.
examples: The magazine’s {circulation} has fallen as readers move online.
wrong: The paper’s circulation is the color of ink it uses.

words.meaning: The people who read a particular publication, or how many of them there are.
examples: The site has a young, well-educated {readership}.
wrong: The readership of the paper is the people who print it.

words.meaning: Interesting or important enough to be reported as news.
examples: Editors decide which events are {newsworthy}.
wrong: The story was so newsworthy that no paper wanted to print it.

words.meaning: A piece of secret information given as a warning or lead, often to police or journalists.
examples: Acting on an anonymous {tip-off}, the reporter visited the warehouse.
wrong: The tip-off gave the journalist no information or lead at all.

words.meaning: Said privately to a journalist and not meant to be published or quoted.
examples: The official spoke {off the record} about the talks.
wrong: She spoke off the record, so the paper printed her quote with her name.

words.meaning: Reports about an event that is happening now or has only just happened.
examples: We interrupt this program with {breaking news} from the capital.
wrong: The breaking news was a story about events from twenty years ago.

words.meaning: Photographers who follow famous people to take pictures of them to sell.
examples: The {paparazzi} waited outside the hotel for the star.
wrong: The paparazzi are shy photographers who never follow celebrities.

words.meaning: A particular point of view that affects how news is presented.
examples: The report had a clear political {slant}.
wrong: Its slant made the article perfectly neutral.

words.meaning: A person or group that controls what information reaches the public.
examples: Editors used to be the main {gatekeepers} of the news.
wrong: As a gatekeeper, he had no say over what got published.

words.meaning: To mix personal opinion into a report that should only give facts.
examples: A news reporter should not {editorialize} in a straight news story.
wrong: He editorialized by sticking strictly to the facts and giving no opinion.

words.meaning: Television or online content that mixes news and information with entertainment.
examples: Critics say the channel offers {infotainment} rather than serious news.
wrong: The program was pure infotainment: a dry list of statistics with no entertainment.

words.meaning: An official statement given to journalists by an organization.
examples: The company announced the merger in a {press release}.
wrong: A press release is a secret memo that journalists are never shown.

words.meaning: A meeting where someone makes an announcement and answers reporters’ questions.
examples: The coach held a {press conference} after the match.
wrong: At the press conference, no reporters were allowed to ask anything.

words.meaning: An organization that publishes or broadcasts news, such as a paper, channel or website.
examples: Several {media outlets} reported the story within minutes.
wrong: A media outlet is a socket for charging your phone.

words.meaning: The main presenter of a news program on TV or radio.
examples: The evening news {anchor} has been on air for twenty years.
wrong: The anchor never appears on screen or speaks during the broadcast.

words.meaning: A person or group that checks that companies or governments behave properly.
examples: A consumer {watchdog} warned about the faulty heaters.
wrong: The watchdog helped the firm hide its illegal practices.

words.meaning: A short, catchy quote from a speech or interview used in news reports.
examples: His one-line {sound bite} was played on every channel.
wrong: The sound bite was a three-hour recording of the full speech.

words.meaning: An expert who often gives opinions on a subject in the media.
examples: Political {pundits} predicted a close result.
wrong: The pundit refused ever to give an opinion on the subject.
